newsitem.title: FRANCE: FIGURE SKATING-ISU TO CONSIDER CLEARING SCORING SYSTEM.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-ISU TO CONSIDER CLEARING SCORING SYSTEM.

text.p: The International Skating Union (ISU) promised on Saturday to look into ways of making figure skating results more easily understandable to the public.

ISU president Ottavio Cinquanta was reacting to the men's result at the European championships on Thursday, when Olympic champion Alexei Urmanov of Russia took the lead only after the final skater, who did not get among the medals, had finished.
"The fact that millions of spectators at Bercy or watching on television did not understand the system of judging does not mean the system is wrong," Cinquanta told a news conference.
"But it does mean the ISU must do something to ensure the spectators are not in that position again. It is time the ISU took the initiative to avoid this happening."
He expressed confidence that proposals aimed at overcoming the problem would be submitted to the next full ISU Congress in 1998.
"So many people are complaining, it is clear either we need a new system of a way of clarifying it to the public. This sort of thing seems to happen every few years."
Urmanov was second behind Viacheslav Zagorodniuk of Ukraine when the last skater, Andrei Vlascenko of Germany, began.
After he finished, Urmanov rose to first, Zagorodniuk dropped to third and Philippe Candeloro advanced two places to second. Vlascenko plunged from third to sixth.
The current judging system is based on placements of skaters in the short and free programmes of the event. France are believed to have already submitted a proposal to bring in a points system.
But the chairman of the ISU's figure skating technical committee, Sally-Ann Stapleford, defended the present judging system.
"It is the fairest and best available," she said.

Cinquanta said the ISU was also considering ways of altering the static position of ice dancers through the various stages of their event, where there were few changes to the order after the first compulsory dance.

"It is easier to fall in figure skating than in ice dancing so it is not as easy for one couple to beat another. But we must do something and we are thinking of ways to giving more variety in results," he said.
Cinquanta said the new Four Continents championship, announced earlier, would begin in 1999.
It is designed to give skaters from the other continents a competition equivalent to the European Championships. Prize money would be awarded in line with other ISU competitions, he said.
